_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: It is Rabbi Elazar, who says: an unmarried man who has intercourse etc.: he calls [a woman who had] intercourse of promiscuity a “prostitute.” Therefore her payment is also forbidden, since the term “payment of a prostitute” applies to it. And I [Abaye], who said [that the payment of a Jewish prostitute is permitted], hold like the Rabbis.
gershom:a1.1: He has made her a prostitute: and her payment is forbidden, even though betrothal takes effect with her.
gershom:a2.1: If it is Rabbi Elazar: why specifically teach “for example, a widow to a High Priest”? Let it teach “for example, an unmarried woman,” with whom betrothal certainly takes effect. Why does it say “for example, a widow”?
rashi:a2.1: It is the paradigm: had it stated an unmarried woman, I would have said: an unmarried woman, yes [her payment is forbidden], since there is no prohibition involved; but the payment of any woman who is forbidden to him should not be forbidden, since the verse writes “prostitute,” and the ordinary prostitute is [the case of] an unmarried man with an unmarried woman, according to Rabbi Elazar.
rashi:a2.2:
And it is the paradigm: [one might think it comes] to teach that payment is forbidden only with an unmarried man and an unmarried woman, but not with a widow, who is forbidden to a High Priest; it teaches us [otherwise].
Another version: whose view is this, which teaches that the payment of a widow to a High Priest is forbidden? It is Rabbi Akiva, who says in chapter HaḤoletz [Yevamot] that betrothal does not take effect with those liable for negative prohibitions; therefore they are like the forbidden relations punishable by karet.
And according to Rava, who says that [the payment of] every prostitute is payment, why does it teach specifically “for example, a widow”? [It should teach] even an unmarried woman, since Rava does not expound this word “abomination” as Abaye does. [The answer is that, like a widow,] a prostitute too is not forbidden until he says to her explicitly, “Here is payment for you”; but without specifying, it is a mere gift, since she does not become a prostitute through one act of intercourse without specification. This is unlike Rabbi Elazar. But where she was a prostitute from the outset, according to Rava too it is payment even without specification, even [if she is] unmarried.
gershom:a3.1: It needed to state a widow: for it might enter your mind to say that, since it is the paradigm, this [ruling] of Rabbi Elazar, who says “he has made her a prostitute,” I would have said that all are derived from here: just as an unmarried woman, with whom there is no prohibition of impurity and no negative prohibition, but only that he had intercourse with her not for the sake of marriage, and with whom betrothal takes effect, her payment is forbidden, so too anyone similar to an unmarried woman, with no negative prohibition and with whom betrothal takes effect, her payment is forbidden. But a widow and a divorcée, even though betrothal takes effect with them, since there is a negative prohibition with them, I might say their payment is not forbidden. It teaches us [otherwise]. That is why it needed to teach “for example, a widow etc.,” [whose payments] are forbidden. [The printed text here is corrupt; we follow the editors’ corrections.]
gershom:a4.1: Another version: Abaye could say to you: this last clause is Rabbi Akiva’s, who says betrothal does not take effect with those liable for negative prohibitions. And it says that every prostitute with whom betrothal does not take effect, that is, forbidden relations and a gentile woman, like a widow to a High Priest, with whom betrothal does not take effect [according to him], her payment is forbidden; but a Jewish prostitute, with whom betrothal does take effect, her payment is permitted.
gershom:a5.1: And according to Rava, who says that even though betrothal takes effect, as with a Jewish prostitute, her payment is forbidden: why does the last clause teach specifically “for example, a widow to a High Priest”? He holds that the payment of every Jewish prostitute is forbidden, even an unmarried woman who is not forbidden to a priest.
gershom:a6.1: Rava could say to you: it teaches “for example, a widow” because he holds [that a prostitute is] similar to a widow. Just as with a widow, if a priest had intercourse with her without specification, without warning, he is not flogged, so too a prostitute: if he had intercourse with her without specification and afterwards gave her [something], it is not payment [and she is not a prostitute] until he says to her explicitly, “Here is payment for you,” [and she accepted it as payment]. This excludes Rabbi Elazar, who says he has made her a prostitute even without specification.
gershom:a7.1: But where: she was a prostitute from the outset, because another man had already said to her, “Here is payment for you,” and she accepted it; then even if another man had intercourse with her without specification and afterwards gave her [something] without specification, her payment is forbidden, since she was a prostitute from the outset.
rashi:a3.1: Is permitted: so why do the Rabbis say it is payment? There is no tanna who forbids the payment of a woman who is permitted [to the man] except Rabbi Elazar alone.
gershom:a8.1: But a maidservant is permitted to a slave: to him. What prohibition is there in this, that it should be payment? Why is this called payment?
rashi:a3.2: With him: with the Jew himself, and to him a maidservant is forbidden.
rashi:a3.3: A refined expression: and “slave” means the organ that serves [in intercourse]. [The note ends with an abbreviation, כ״ש, whose meaning here is unclear.]
gershom:a9.1: Rav Huna said: he means “and let her lodge with him himself,” which is a prohibition. Another version: who is “my slave”? He himself; that is, he means “let her lodge with me,” and when he says “my slave” he uses a refined expression, that is, he does not want to say explicitly “let her lodge with me.” [If so, that he means himself, why does Rabbi say it is not payment? There is a prohibition here, of a Jew with a maidservant. Rather, the “my slave” of the mishna is a Hebrew slave, who is permitted to a Canaanite maidservant. If so, what is the reason of the Rabbis, who say it is payment?]
rashi:a5.1: A maidservant is permitted to a Hebrew slave: as it is written: “For double the hire of a hired worker has he served you” (Deuteronomy 15:18): he works both by day and by night, for he fathered children for his master from his maidservant.
gershom:a10.1: For example, where he has no wife and children: the Hebrew slave. As it is taught: if the Hebrew slave had a wife and children when he entered [servitude], his master gives etc. If he has no wife and children, his master does not give him a Canaanite maidservant, because it is written: “If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself” (Exodus 21:3): he had no wife; “he shall go out by himself”: that he should not give him a Canaanite maidservant. And if he gave her to him, and [a man] said to his fellow, “Here is a lamb, and let [your] maidservant lodge with my slave,” this is payment, for it is a prohibition, since he had no wife and children.
rashi:a5.2: His master does not give him etc.: as it is written: “If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself” (Exodus 21:3). And Rabbi, who says it is not payment, does not hold this reasoning, for in his view, even if he has no wife and children, his master certainly may give him a Canaanite maidservant.
rashi:a5.3: If he has a wife and children, his master gives him a Canaanite maidservant: even against the slave’s will, for it is a decree of Scripture, as it is written: “If he is a married man” (Exodus 21:3), and after it is written: “If his master gives him a wife” (Exodus 21:4).
rashi:a7.1: Mishna. Those against the dog are forbidden: for sacrifice, since they are the price of a dog.
gershom:a11.1: If those against the dog: all ten are forbidden, for we say that each and every one belongs against the dog, as is explained in the Gemara; and those nine that are with the dog are permitted.
rashi:a8.1: Payment of a dog: [he says,] “Here is this lamb, and let your female dog spend the night with me.”
rashi:a8.2: The price of a prostitute: he exchanged a lamb for a prostitute, and acquired her as his maidservant with that lamb.
rashi:a8.3: Their offspring: of the price and the payment.
rashi:a8.4: Are permitted: as it is said: “both of them,” and not their offspring.
rashi:a9.1: Gemara. “And have not set their prices high”: evidently meḥir, “price,” means damim, the value [given for something].
gershom:a12.1: “And have not set their prices high”: their exchanges.
rashi:a10.1: Say instead payment: actual payment, so that “the price of a dog” is payment.
gershom:a13.1: Say: what is “the price of a dog”? Actual payment for a dog, for example where he said to him: “Here is this lamb, and let your maidservant lodge with my dog.”
rashi:a10.2: And it answers: two and not three: [that is, payment of a prostitute, and payment and price of a dog].
gershom:a14.1: If so, there are three: payment of a prostitute, payment of a dog and price of a dog; yet it writes “both of them,” and not three.
gershom:a15.1: And the one who said “say [etc.]” would answer you: there is no refutation from “two and not three.” Do we say payment and price, that is, that “payment” also applies to the dog, which would make three? We are saying payment and not price, that is: what is “price”? Payment of a dog. That makes two.
gershom:a16.1: If so: as you said, what is “the price of a dog”? [Payment.] Then let the verse say “the payment of a prostitute or a dog,” which would also imply payment for the dog. Rather, since the Merciful One wrote “the payment of a prostitute and the price of a dog,” learn from it that “price” is what the Merciful One says about the dog, which means an exchange, and not payment.
rashi:a12.1: “And the price of a dog” is written: that is, since the vav is written with “and the price,” it adds to the first matter, and both its exchange and its payment are forbidden.
gershom:a17.1: Another version: “the price of a dog” is the payment of a dog, and not an exchange.
gershom:a18.1: If so, let the verse write “the payment of a prostitute or a dog,” with no need for “price.” [Answer:] say [that it reads] “the payment of a prostitute and the price of a dog,” for the vav of “and the price” adds to the first matter, and read it thus: “the payment and the price of a dog”; that is, that the name of both payment and price apply to a dog.
gershom:a19.1: That cannot enter your mind: “an abomination to the Lord… both of them” it writes, two and not three. And if it were as you said, there would be three: payment of a prostitute, and payment and price of a dog.
tosafot:a13.1:
In brief: “And let the rest be permitted”: that is, by the principle of bererah, retroactive clarification. This fits the Ri, who rules throughout the Talmud that bererah applies; but according to Rabbeinu Tam, who rules that it does not, how can the Gemara ask so simply? Answer: since there are tanna’im who hold bererah, it asks why the mishna should be established against them.
A further difficulty: here it implies that when a forbidden item is mixed with permitted ones, one takes out the forbidden amount and relies on bererah to say that this is the forbidden one that was removed, as in one who buys wine from the Samaritans and says “two log that I will separate are tithe” (Demai 7:4), relying on bererah that what he drinks is non-sacred; and as with the three women who bought their pairs of birds in partnership, one of which died, where the Gemara asks simply in Yoma (55b), “Let us take four zuz and throw them away, and let the rest be permitted.” If so, for every forbidden item mixed with permitted ones we should rely on bererah, take out the forbidden amount and let the rest be permitted. And with offerings mixed with an ox that is to be stoned, where we say they must all die (Zevaḥim 70b): granted that living creatures are significant and are not nullified, still let us take one of them and let the rest be permitted!
My teacher HaRaMaR says a great rule in this: wherever the forbidden item was identified first and afterwards mixed with permitted ones, we do not rely on bererah, since it was mixed as a forbidden item. But in these cases the mixture was of permitted things, for the forbidden item was not identified before it was mixed, and the prohibition came into being after the mixture; then we rely on bererah. [See Tosafot Bekhorot 56b, and Tosafot Sota 18a.] Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a21.1: Another version: why are all those against the dog forbidden? Let one take one of those that are with the dog to be forbidden, and let the rest be permitted.
rashi:a13.1:
Than one of them: that among those set against it there is no lamb worth the dog’s value, so that now the dog’s value is mixed into all of them. For example, those set against it are each worth a dinar, making ten dinars, and the nine with it are each worth a dinar less a ma’ah, that is, nine dinars less nine ma’ot, and the dog is worth a dinar and nine ma’ot: that makes ten dinars. It follows that in nine of those set against it [part] of the dog’s value is found, and the tenth is wholly against it.
In the language of the Jerusalem Talmud: for example, each of those set against it is worth four zuz and half a fifth of a zuz, making forty-one zuz among them all, and those with it are worth only four zuz each, making thirty-six zuz, and the dog is worth five, making forty-one. It follows that in each of nine of the ten set against it there is half a fifth of the dog’s value, and the tenth is wholly against it.
gershom:a20.1: Here we are dealing with: for example, where the dog’s value exceeds each one of them that are set against it, so that the dog’s excess belongs to all of them, to make up its value. Therefore all those set against the dog are forbidden.
gershom:a22.1: Rav Ashi said: here we are dealing with [a case] where each of all ten lambs is worth four zuz and half a fifth, and the dog is worth five zuz, so that the dog’s extra zuz, that fifth one, extends into all of them; for the half-fifths of all of them come to one zuz, which is that fifth zuz by which the dog is worth more. And this last version explains the “excess” of the first version. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text gives this answer in the name of Rav Ashi; on the daf it is unattributed.]
gershom:a23.1: Payment of a dog, as we said, and the price of a prostitute, for example where he exchanged a lamb for a prostitute: these are permitted. “Two”: two and not four. The four are payment of a prostitute, payment of a dog, price of a prostitute and price of a dog.
rashi:b1.1: There is no prostitution with an animal: as the mishna teaches, payment of a dog is permitted.
tosafot:b1.1:
In brief: Rashi explains that the question concerns the mishna’s ruling that payment of a dog is permitted. This is difficult: did he not know that the mishna expounds the verse, “two and not four”? And what is the answer “the verse would not have omitted…”: was Rav Ashi giving a new reasoning not found in the mishna? And when the Gemara cites the baraita of “two and not four,” why not cite the mishna, which teaches the same?
My teacher’s view: Rav Aḥa from Parzakya [so Tosafot read the name] certainly knew the mishna and the verse, and it was obvious to him that payment given for a female dog is not payment, because of “two and not four.” But he was asking the reverse: if a man gives a woman payment so that his dog may lie with her, is intercourse with a dog called intercourse of prostitution or not? Even though payment that a man gives for a female dog is not forbidden, perhaps payment for a dog’s intercourse with a woman is forbidden. And it answers: the verse would not have failed to write “the payment of a prostitute or a dog,” [covering] both the payment a man gives her and the payment for a dog with her. The wording is somewhat forced.
Then it cites the baraita: just as a man’s intercourse with an animal is not intercourse of prostitution, so an animal’s with a woman is not called prostitution. It did not cite the mishna, because a mishna does not usually explain; but a baraita would have said so explicitly had the payment of a woman who was with a dog been forbidden. And in Yevamot (59b) it is evident that Rav Aḥa’s statement was said about a woman with a dog: there is an incident there of a young woman in Hitlu who was sweeping the house, and a dog copulated with her from behind; the case came before the Sages and they ruled her fit [to marry a priest], and about that incident Rav Aḥa from Parzakya asked, “From where is this matter…?” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b1.1: There is no prostitution with an animal: to forbid its payment.
gershom:b2.1: For if it were so, the verse would not have omitted to write “the payment of a prostitute or a dog,” so that “payment” would apply to the dog too. Another version: since it did not write “the payment and the price of a dog and of a prostitute,” it does not apply payment and price both to the dog and to the prostitute.
rashi:b2.1: It is also taught so: “From where” etc.: we read this. [It is the mishna; but because the baraita teaches “From where is it for payment…” and explains it explicitly, he cites it for that reason. This is uncertain, and it seems to me that we do not read it.]
gershom:b3.1: It is also taught so: that there is no prostitution with an animal.
gershom:b4.1: For if you say so, to apply what is said of this one to that one, so that payment of a dog and price of a prostitute are forbidden, there would be four.
gershom:b5.1: And their offspring: of the payment and the price, are permitted.
gershom:b6.1: As it is said, “even both of them”: them, and not their offspring.
rashi:b4.1: The offspring of a set-aside and a worshipped animal is permitted: for he set aside only the mother, and they worshipped only the mother.
gershom:b7.1: What is the reason? He set aside its mother: that is, he intended to set aside only its mother and not the fetus.
tosafot:b4.1:
That he is pleased with its girth: this is puzzling. Here, with a worshipped animal, we forbid the offspring of a worshipped animal; and in Avoda Zara (46b) it asks: one who bows down to standing grain, what is [its] fine flour for meal offerings? Does a change [of form] apply to a worshipped item or not? And it cites this statement of Rava, that the offspring of a worshipped animal is forbidden, and answers there: at first it was an animal and now it is an animal, it was merely that a door was closed before it; but fine flour was at first wheat and is now fine flour. Evidently we are more lenient with a change than with an offspring. Yet with a prostitute’s payment, the reasoning of Beit Shammai is the reverse: they said that a change stays as it was, and wheat that was made into fine flour is forbidden, while for offspring they agree it is permitted, from the exposition “them, and not their offspring.”
There is a reason to distinguish. Certainly with idolatry the offspring is forbidden, as explained here, that he is pleased with its girth and intends to bow down to the whole girth; but one who bows down to standing grain intends to bow down only to what he sees, the wheat, and not the fine flour. With a payment, however, her intent is for the principal and its increase in value; therefore with an animal, the prostitute’s intent is for the animal and not the offspring, and with grain, her intent is for the fine flour, which is the main thing.
gershom:b8.1: [The offspring of a] set-aside [and worshipped animal] is forbidden: for the fetus benefits from what its mother benefits.
gershom:b9.1: What is the reason? He is pleased with its swelling and fattening: that is, he is pleased that when the animal is pregnant it looks fat and swollen and appears more important for idol worship. Therefore he is pleased with the fetus, and it is forbidden.
gershom:b11.1: If you wish, say it is reasoning: with idol worship he is pleased with its girth, from the excrement inside it, which makes it look fat; therefore [the excrement] is forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b12.1: With an ox that is to be stoned, he is not pleased with its girth from its excrement, for it is about to die; therefore she is betrothed.
gershom:b10.1: Anything that you create from it is like it: anything that comes from it is forbidden, and she is not betrothed.
rashi:b8.1: Mishna. He gave her consecrated items: payment does not take effect on them, as is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b9.1: He gave her birds: non-sacred ones; these are thereafter forbidden for sacrifice.
rashi:b10.1: The offspring of a tereifa shall not be sacrificed: but for an ordinary person all agree it is permitted, since it did not grow from its body.
tosafot:b10.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: the offspring of a tereifa shall not be sacrificed: Rashi explains that for an ordinary person all agree it is permitted, since it did not grow from its body. This is not correct, for in chapter Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 58a) it is explained explicitly that it is forbidden even to an ordinary person, and that they disagree about the altar is to tell you the strength of the Rabbis’ view, that they permit it even for the altar. Therefore it seems that [according to Rabbi Eliezer] it is forbidden even to an ordinary person, and he says “shall not be sacrificed” because of the Rabbis, who say “it may be sacrificed.”
rashi:b11.1: Aspork: the name of a place.
gershom:b13.1: [It seems that Rabbeinu Gershom read here in the Gemara: “What is the reason that if he gave her money they are permitted?”] For it is written “payment of a prostitute,” and not “the payment”; and it is not written “with payment,” that is, anything bought with the payment. Moreover, if you said that an animal she bought with her payment is forbidden, that would be like their offspring, which come from the payment, and the mishna teaches that their offspring are permitted: the verse says “even both of them,” them and not their offspring. “Even” is an inclusion, to include their changed forms, such as wheat that she made into fine flour: even though they changed, they are forbidden.
gershom:b14.1: And Beit Hillel expound thus: “both of them”: them, and not their changed forms; their changed forms and their offspring are permitted. And “even,” which we said comes to include, is difficult for Beit Hillel, since for them it includes nothing.
gershom:b15.1: Excluding a heifer, which does not come into the House: for all its rites are done on the Mount of Anointing, so one may bring it from a payment.
rashi:b14.2: And plates: overlay for the altar, if he gave her gold.
gershom:b16.1: And the Rabbis say: “House” includes the plates: that one does not bring [them] from a payment, even behind the Hall of the Ark Cover, outside, to plaster the wall, for there too we call it “the House of the Lord.”
rashi:b15.1: Behind the Hall of the Ark Cover: as we say in the first chapter of Yoma (21a), eleven cubits were left in the courtyard behind the wall of the Hall of the Ark Cover. Even there, where the sanctity is lighter, payment is forbidden, if there is building to be done and he gave her stones as her payment.
gershom:b17.1: He gave her consecrated items as her payment, they are permitted; and birds are forbidden, though by right the birds should have been permitted.
gershom:b18.1: The verse states “for any vow”: to include the bird, which comes as a vow or a gift offering, that payment takes effect on them.
rashi:b17.1: Payment and price take effect on them: as we include in the mishna, “for any vow,” to include the bird.
gershom:b19.1: Excluding an item already vowed: that is, consecrated items, which are already vowed. But a person cannot forbid an item that is not his, for they belong to the Temple; so how would her payment take effect on them?
rashi:b19.1: To one who registers [her] for his Paschal offering: the case where the verse was needed to exclude it is, for example, where he set aside his Paschal offering and later said to a prostitute, “Be with me, and be registered on my Paschal offering as your payment.” And since Rabbi says a person may register others [on his Paschal offering] if he needs money for something, evidently it is his property, and one might say that payment takes effect on it. That is why “for any vow” was needed, to exclude what is vowed.
gershom:b20.1: Rav Hoshaya said: it speaks of consecrated items that are in his possession, such as his Paschal offering, where he registers her on his Paschal offering as her payment; and it is according to Rabbi, who holds that he may acquire from his Paschal offering what he needs.
rashi:b19.2: “And if the household be too little”: he expounds it thus: that his household became too little, that he does not have what he needs [to buy for the needs of the Paschal offering, that is,] “for a lamb [mihyot miseh]”: sustain him from the lamb, that he may register others with him on his Paschal offering and they give him money.
gershom:b21.1: As it is taught: “And if the household be too little for a lamb”: that is, if the household lacks, so that he does not have what he needs to prepare the Paschal offering, such as wood or spices, “sustain him from the lamb.”
rashi:b20.1: From the needs of eating: if the household lacks the needs of eating, he may receive his sustenance and food from the lamb. If he has nothing to eat, “sustain him from the lamb”; if he has no wood to roast it, that too is “from the needs of eating,” and [the rule] “sustain him” [applies]. [The last words of the printed note, “and not sustain him from the lamb,” seem to belong to the next note.]
rashi:b20.2: And not from the needs of a purchase: if he wants to trade, and his household lacks the means for that purchase, so that he has nothing to pay for it, he does not register others on his Paschal offering for that.
gershom:b22.1: From the needs of eating and not from the needs of a purchase: that is, if he lacks what he needs to prepare his meal, he may take money from others and register them on his Paschal offering, and buy wood with the money for preparing the eating of his Paschal offering; but he may not buy anything else with that money, such as a cloak or clothing.
gershom:b23.1:
Rabbi says: even from the needs of a purchase: that if he needs a cloak or something else, he registers others etc., and the money is non-sacred and he may use it for his needs, for it is on this condition that the Jewish people consecrated their Paschal offerings, that if he needs something he may register others with him and use the money for his needs. By the reasoning of Rabbi, who says even from the needs of a purchase, payment would take effect on it, had the verse not excluded it with “vow.”
[Rabbi Eliezer holds that when both this and that cause something, it is forbidden: even though this offspring comes from one permitted side, its father, which has no prohibition, nevertheless, since its mother is forbidden, both together cause this offspring, and it is forbidden. And the Rabbis of the mishna hold that when both this and that cause something, it is permitted. But if they became pregnant etc.]
rashi:b23.1: A fetus is the thigh of its mother: and so it was itself the object of bestiality.
tosafot:b23.1: But if they were the object of bestiality and then became pregnant, all agree they are permitted: that is, [because] when both this and that cause something, it is permitted. This is difficult, for we find that Rabbi Eliezer holds in chapter Kol Sha’ah (Pesaḥim 27a) that when both this and that cause something, it is forbidden. One may answer that there it deals with an item forbidden even to an ordinary person, and here it deals with a prohibition for the altar alone. [See Tosafot Sanhedrin 80b, beginning “ela.”]
rashi:b24.1: Both this and that cause: the male that mated with this animal, and it [the mother], caused the offspring to come about, so a prohibition and a permission caused it, for its father is permitted and its mother forbidden.
gershom:b24.1: Another version: the dispute is where they were the object of bestiality when they were consecrated, even though they became pregnant afterwards. Rabbi Elazar [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text, for Rabbi Eliezer] holds that we say it is a degradation to offer their offspring, since they were the object of bestiality when consecrated. But if they were the object of bestiality when they were non-sacred, and after that he consecrated them, since they changed, all agree they are permitted. [The printed note then repeats itself: their pregnancy, since they changed when he consecrated them, all agree they are permitted.]
gershom:b25.1: And Rava said that Rav Naḥman said etc. And according to the one who says in Sheḥitat Ḥullin that a tereifa does not give birth, that is, does not become pregnant, you find this case of the offspring of a tereifa that is taught [in the mishna] where it became pregnant and afterwards became a tereifa.
